name: History & Civics
tagline: How we got here, and how we live together.

nodes.title: Family and Past
nodes.goal: Understand yesterday, today, tomorrow and family history.
nodes.kid_text: Every day has a yesterday, a today, and a tomorrow! Yesterday already happened, today is right now, and tomorrow is coming next. Your family has a past too: your grandma was once a little kid just like you, and one day you might have kids of your own. Ask a grownup to tell you a story about when they were small.

quiz.prompt: Which one already happened? 🕐
choices: Yesterday
Today
Tomorrow
quiz.answer: Yesterday
quiz.say: Which one already happened — yesterday, today, or tomorrow?
quiz.explain: Yes! Yesterday is already finished, and tomorrow has not come yet.

quiz.prompt: Right now is called what? ⏰
choices: Today
Yesterday
Tomorrow
quiz.answer: Today
quiz.say: Right now, this very moment — is it today, yesterday, or tomorrow?
quiz.explain: Right! The moment you are in is always called today.

quiz.prompt: Was Grandma once a little kid? 👵
choices: Yes
No
quiz.answer: Yes
quiz.say: Was your grandma once a little kid, just like you? Say yes, or no.
quiz.explain: Yes! Every grownup was small once, a long time ago.

quiz.prompt: Which day has not come yet? 🌅
choices: Today
Tomorrow
Yesterday
quiz.answer: Tomorrow
quiz.say: Which day has not come yet — today, tomorrow, or yesterday?
quiz.explain: Yes! Tomorrow is still waiting for us, it has not happened yet.

quiz.prompt: You ate breakfast this morning. It is? 🥣
choices: Already done
Happening now
Still to come
quiz.answer: Already done
quiz.say: You ate your breakfast this morning. Is that already done, happening now, or still to come?
quiz.explain: Right! Breakfast this morning is finished, so it is in the past.

quiz.prompt: Who was a little kid first? 👴👨👦
choices: You
Dad
Grandpa
quiz.answer: Grandpa
quiz.say: Who was a little kid first of all — you, your dad, or your grandpa?
quiz.explain: Grandpa was little first, then your dad, and then you.

quiz.prompt: Grandma, Mom, you. Who came last? 👶
choices: Grandma
Mom
You
quiz.answer: You
quiz.say: First grandma was born, then mom, then you. Who came last — grandma, mom, or you?
quiz.explain: You came last! You are the newest one in the family story.

nodes.title: People Who Help
nodes.goal: Meet the helpers in a community.
nodes.kid_text: Your neighborhood is full of helpers doing important jobs! Doctors help you feel better, firefighters put out fires, and mail carriers bring letters to your door. Teachers help you learn and bus drivers take you places. When you wave to a helper, you are thanking someone who makes your community work.

quiz.prompt: Who puts out fires? 🔥
choices: Firefighter
Shopkeeper
Bricklayer
quiz.answer: Firefighter
quiz.say: Who comes to put out a fire? Is it a firefighter, a shopkeeper, or a bricklayer?
quiz.explain: Yes! Firefighters use big hoses to put fires out.

quiz.prompt: Who helps when you feel sick? 🤒
choices: Doctor
Mail carrier
Baker
quiz.answer: Doctor
quiz.say: When you feel sick, who helps you feel better — a doctor, a mail carrier, or a baker?
quiz.explain: That's right, doctors help us get well again.

quiz.prompt: Who brings letters to your door? ✉️
choices: Mail carrier
Bus driver
Shopkeeper
quiz.answer: Mail carrier
quiz.say: Who brings letters right to your door? Is it a mail carrier, a bus driver, or a shopkeeper?
quiz.explain: Yes! Mail carriers carry letters to every house.

quiz.prompt: Who helps you learn at school? 📚
choices: Teacher
Builder
Firefighter
quiz.answer: Teacher
quiz.say: Who helps you learn new things at school — a teacher, a builder, or a firefighter?
quiz.explain: Yes! Teachers help us read, count, and learn every day.

quiz.prompt: Who drives the school bus? 🚌
choices: Bus driver
Pilot
Baker
quiz.answer: Bus driver
quiz.say: Who drives the big school bus — a bus driver, a pilot, or a baker?
quiz.explain: Right! Bus drivers take lots of children safely to school.

quiz.prompt: Who bakes fresh bread? 🍞
choices: Nurse
Baker
Doctor
quiz.answer: Baker
quiz.say: Who bakes the fresh bread we eat? A nurse, a baker, or a doctor?
quiz.explain: Yes! Bakers get up early to bake warm bread for everyone.

quiz.prompt: Who helps keep our streets safe? 🚦
choices: Police
Singer
Waiter
quiz.answer: Police
quiz.say: Who helps keep our streets safe? Is it police, a singer, or a waiter?
quiz.explain: That's right, police officers help keep our neighborhood safe.

nodes.title: Long, Long Ago
nodes.goal: Imagine life before cars and phones.
nodes.kid_text: A long, long time ago, before you were born, there were no cars, no phones, and no lights that turn on with a switch! People walked everywhere or rode horses, and they lit candles when it got dark at night. To talk to a friend far away, they had to write a letter and wait many days. Close your eyes and imagine a night with only a candle and the stars.

quiz.prompt: Long ago there were no cars. What then? ⏳
choices: Horse
Plane
Train
quiz.answer: Horse
quiz.say: Long ago there were no cars. What did people ride instead — a horse, a plane, or a train?
quiz.explain: Yes! People walked, or they rode horses to get places.

quiz.prompt: Long ago, what made light at night? 🌃
choices: Candle
Light switch
Flashlight
quiz.answer: Candle
quiz.say: Long ago at night, what gave people light — a candle, a light switch, or a flashlight?
quiz.explain: That's right, they lit candles, because switches had not been made yet.

quiz.prompt: No phones! How to reach a far friend? 🏡
choices: Letter
E-mail
Text
quiz.answer: Letter
quiz.say: Long ago there were no phones. To reach a faraway friend, did people send a letter, an e-mail, or a text?
quiz.explain: Yes! They wrote a letter and waited many days for an answer.

quiz.prompt: Long ago, was there TV? 📺
choices: Yes
No
quiz.answer: No
quiz.say: Long, long ago, did people have television? Say yes, or no.
quiz.explain: No! Televisions had not been invented yet, so people told stories.

quiz.prompt: Which came first, long ago? ⏳
choices: Horse
Truck
Bicycle
quiz.answer: Horse
quiz.say: Which one did people have first, long ago — the horse, the truck, or the bicycle?
quiz.explain: Horses came first! Bicycles and trucks were made much, much later.

quiz.prompt: Long ago, how were clothes washed? 🧺
choices: By hand
Washing machine
Dryer
quiz.answer: By hand
quiz.say: Long ago, how did people wash their clothes — by hand, in a washing machine, or in a dryer?
quiz.explain: Yes! They scrubbed clothes by hand, because washing machines were not made yet.

quiz.prompt: No lights! When did people sleep? 🛏️
choices: When dark
At midday
At sunrise
quiz.answer: When dark
quiz.say: Long ago there were no lights. When did people go to sleep — when dark, at midday, or at sunrise?
quiz.explain: Right, when the sun went down and it got dark, it was bedtime.

nodes.title: Timelines
nodes.goal: Order events in time; read a timeline.
nodes.kid_text: A timeline is like a road that shows when things happened, with the oldest things first and the newest things last. If you drew your own timeline, being a baby would come first, then learning to walk, then starting school. We read a timeline from left to right, just like reading a story. Try putting three things you did today in the right order!

quiz.prompt: On your timeline, which is first? 👶🧒🧑
quiz.say: On your own timeline, which comes first — being a baby 👶, being a big kid 🧒, or being a grownup 🧑?
quiz.explain: Right! Baby comes first, because that happened the longest ago.

quiz.prompt: Which way do we read a timeline? 📜
choices: Left to right
Right to left
Top to bottom
quiz.answer: Left to right
quiz.say: Which way do we read a timeline — left to right, right to left, or top to bottom?
quiz.explain: Yes, just like a story, a timeline goes from left to right.

quiz.prompt: A baby grows up. Which comes last? ⏳
choices: Run
Crawl
Walk
quiz.answer: Run
quiz.say: A baby learns to move about. Which one comes last — run, crawl, or walk?
quiz.explain: Yes! First you crawl, then you walk, then you run. Running comes last.

quiz.prompt: On a hen's timeline, which is first? 📅
choices: Hen
Egg
Chick
quiz.answer: Egg
quiz.say: On a hen's timeline, which one comes first — the hen, the egg, or the chick?
quiz.explain: Yes! First there is an egg, then a chick hatches out, and then it grows into a hen.

quiz.prompt: Which meal comes last in the day? 🕐
choices: Dinner
Lunch
Breakfast
quiz.answer: Dinner
quiz.say: Which meal comes last in the day — dinner, lunch, or breakfast?
quiz.explain: Right! Breakfast is in the morning, lunch in the middle of the day, and dinner comes last.

quiz.prompt: On a timeline, oldest goes where? ⬅️
choices: Left
Right
Middle
quiz.answer: Left
quiz.say: On a timeline, does the oldest thing go on the left, on the right, or in the middle?
quiz.explain: Yes! The oldest things start on the left, and newer things follow.

quiz.prompt: A tree grows in three steps. Which is the middle one? ⏳
choices: Sprout
Seed
Tree
quiz.answer: Sprout
quiz.say: A tree grows in three steps. Which one is the middle step — the sprout, the seed, or the tree?
quiz.explain: That's right — first a seed, then a sprout, then a tall tree. The sprout is in the middle.

nodes.title: Ancient Peoples
nodes.goal: Egypt, Mesopotamia and the first cities.
nodes.kid_text: Thousands of years ago, some of the very first cities grew up next to big rivers like the Nile in Egypt. People there learned to farm, build with mud bricks, and even make giant stone pyramids that still stand today! In a place called Mesopotamia, people built the first cities and started writing things down. Living near a river gave people water to drink and to grow their food.

quiz.prompt: The first cities grew next to what? 🏙️
choices: Rivers
Mountains
Deserts
quiz.answer: Rivers
quiz.say: The first cities grew right next to something big. Was it rivers, mountains, or deserts?
quiz.explain: Yes! The first cities grew beside rivers, which gave people water to drink and water for their crops.

quiz.prompt: What did Egypt build from stone? 🏗️
choices: Pyramids
Castles
Bridges
quiz.answer: Pyramids
quiz.say: In Egypt, people built giant things out of heavy stone. Were they pyramids, castles, or bridges?
quiz.explain: Yes! The Egyptians built pyramids out of huge blocks of stone, as tombs for their kings.

quiz.prompt: Which big river is in Egypt? 🏜️
choices: Nile
Amazon
Thames
quiz.answer: Nile
quiz.say: Which big river runs through Egypt — the Nile, the Amazon, or the Thames?
quiz.explain: Yes, the Nile! People farmed and built cities along it.

quiz.prompt: When was ancient Egypt? ⏳
choices: Last week
When Grandma was small
Thousands of years ago
quiz.answer: Thousands of years ago
quiz.say: When did ancient Egypt happen — last week, when grandma was small, or thousands of years ago?
quiz.explain: Yes! Ancient Egypt was thousands of years ago, before your grandparents' grandparents.

quiz.prompt: Ancient houses were built from what? 🏠
choices: Mud bricks
Concrete
Plastic
quiz.answer: Mud bricks
quiz.say: Long ago, what did people build their houses from — mud bricks, concrete, or plastic?
quiz.explain: Right! They shaped mud into bricks and dried them in the sun.

quiz.prompt: Where did writing first start? ✍️
choices: Mesopotamia
Rome
China
quiz.answer: Mesopotamia
quiz.say: Where did people first start writing things down — in Mesopotamia, in Rome, or in China?
quiz.explain: Yes! The first writing we know of was made in Mesopotamia, pressed into soft clay with a reed.

quiz.prompt: Why live beside a river? 🏞️
choices: For water
For a nice view
For snow
quiz.answer: For water
quiz.say: Why did the first people live right beside a river — for water, for a nice view, or for snow?
quiz.explain: That's right, rivers gave them water to drink and to grow food.

nodes.title: Maps and Places
nodes.goal: Continents, oceans and reading a map.
nodes.kid_text: A map is a picture of a place seen from high above, like a bird looking down. Our whole world has seven big pieces of land called continents and huge bodies of water called oceans. Blue on a map usually means water, and green or brown means land. Find where you live on a map, then find the nearest ocean!

quiz.prompt: On a map, blue means what? 🔵
choices: Water
Land
Roads
quiz.answer: Water
quiz.say: On a map, what does the colour blue mean — water, land, or roads?
quiz.explain: That's right, blue shows the oceans, lakes and rivers.

quiz.prompt: How many continents? 🌍
quiz.say: How many big pieces of land, called continents, does our world have? Is it 3, 7, or 10?
quiz.explain: Seven! Seven continents hold all the land on Earth.

quiz.prompt: A map shows a place from where? 🐦
choices: From above
From the side
From below
quiz.answer: From above
quiz.say: A map shows a place from where — from above like a bird, from the side, or from below the ground?
quiz.explain: Yes, a map is what you would see looking down from the sky.

quiz.prompt: On a map, green means what? 🟩
choices: Land
Water
Sky
quiz.answer: Land
quiz.say: On a map, what does the colour green usually mean — land, water, or sky?
quiz.explain: Yes! Green and brown show the land where we walk.

quiz.prompt: Huge salty waters are called what? 🗺️
choices: Oceans
Lakes
Deserts
quiz.answer: Oceans
quiz.say: The huge salty waters on our world are called what — oceans, lakes, or deserts?
quiz.explain: Right! Oceans are the giant salty waters around the continents.

quiz.prompt: Which one is a continent? 🌎
choices: Africa
Pacific
Nile
quiz.answer: Africa
quiz.say: Which one is a continent, a big piece of land — Africa, the Pacific, or the Nile?
quiz.explain: Yes! Africa is a continent. The Pacific is an ocean and the Nile is a river.

quiz.prompt: Which is biggest? 🏠🏙️🌍
choices: House
City
Continent
quiz.answer: Continent
quiz.say: Which one is biggest — a house, a city, or a whole continent?
quiz.explain: A continent! It is so big that maps shrink it down onto paper.

nodes.title: Great Inventions
nodes.goal: The wheel, writing, and fire.
nodes.kid_text: An invention is a brand-new thing someone thought up to make life easier. Long ago people invented the wheel, so heavy things could roll instead of being dragged. They learned to make fire to stay warm and cook food, and they invented writing so ideas could be saved on paper. Every toy and tool you use was once a brand-new idea in somebody's head!

quiz.prompt: Which invention rolls? 🛠️
choices: Wheel
Fire
Writing
quiz.answer: Wheel
quiz.say: Which invention rolls, so heavy things do not have to be dragged — the wheel, fire, or writing?
quiz.explain: Yes! The wheel rolls, and it made moving heavy things much easier.

quiz.prompt: What keeps us warm and cooks food? 🛠️
choices: Fire
Wheel
Writing
quiz.answer: Fire
quiz.say: Which invention keeps people warm and cooks their food — fire, the wheel, or writing?
quiz.explain: Right, fire gave people warmth, light, and hot food.

quiz.prompt: How do we save ideas on paper? 🧠
choices: Writing
Singing
Running
quiz.answer: Writing
quiz.say: How can we save our ideas on paper so people read them later — by writing, by singing, or by running?
quiz.explain: Yes! Writing lets an idea last a very long time.

quiz.prompt: Why can a wheel roll? 🛠️
choices: It is round
It is heavy
It is wooden
quiz.answer: It is round
quiz.say: Why can a wheel roll along the ground — because it is round, because it is heavy, or because it is wooden?
quiz.explain: Yes! Wheels are round, and that is why they can roll.

quiz.prompt: Every toy started as a what? 🧸
choices: New idea
Rock
Shop
quiz.answer: New idea
quiz.say: Every toy and tool started as something. Was it a new idea, a rock, or a shop?
quiz.explain: Right! Someone thought of it first, and then they made it.

quiz.prompt: Books are full of which invention? 🧠
choices: Writing
Fire
Wheel
quiz.answer: Writing
quiz.say: Books are full of which invention — writing, fire, or the wheel?
quiz.explain: Yes! Books are made of writing, so ideas can be read again and again.

quiz.prompt: A brand-new thing someone made? 🛠️
choices: Invention
Song
Story
quiz.answer: Invention
quiz.say: When someone thinks up a brand-new thing and makes it, is it an invention, a song, or a story?
quiz.explain: That's right, a brand-new helpful thing is called an invention.

nodes.title: Ancient Civilizations
nodes.goal: Greece, Rome, China, India and the Americas.

quiz.prompt: Ancient Greece and ancient Rome both left ideas we still use today. Which of these is something the Romans are especially famous for spreading across their empire?
quiz.answer: A network of roads and aqueducts
quiz.explain: Rome built durable roads and aqueducts to move armies, goods, and water across its vast empire.
choices: The first known system of writing
A network of roads and aqueducts
Gunpowder and cannon technology
The invention of paper and ink

quiz.prompt: A civilization builds cities beside a great river, invents a form of writing, and is ruled by kings whose family holds power for generations. Of the early civilizations, which is best described this way?
quiz.answer: Ancient China along the Yellow River
quiz.explain: Cities on the Yellow River, an early script, and dynasties in which power passed inside one family — all three fit. Athens had no such kings, the Indus Valley left no ruler we can name, and the Maya built away from any great river.
choices: Ancient Athens, governed by an assembly of its citizens
Ancient China along the Yellow River
The Indus Valley, which left no ruler on record
The Maya cities, built in rainforest far from a great river

quiz.prompt: A Roman legion marches 20 Roman miles a day along a paved road. A messenger on horseback covers 60 miles a day on the same road. The road from one city to another is 240 miles long. How many more days does the legion take than the messenger?
quiz.explain: The legion takes 240 / 20 = 12 days and the messenger 240 / 60 = 4 days, a difference of 8 days.

quiz.prompt: Archaeologists digging cities of the Indus Valley find streets laid out in a grid, brick drains running under the roads, and bricks of the same size in towns hundreds of kilometres apart. What does this best suggest about the people who built them?
quiz.answer: They planned their towns together and used shared standards
choices: Each town was built by a separate group working to its own design
They planned their towns together and used shared standards
One ruler must have personally designed every one of the towns
Brick making was the only craft these towns ever practised
quiz.explain: Bricks of one size and a repeated street plan across hundreds of kilometres point to agreed standards rather than independent invention in each town — and standards can be shared without any single person designing everything.

quiz.prompt: The Inca ruled a huge mountain empire without an alphabet. Which method did Inca officials use to keep records of goods and people?
quiz.answer: Knotted cords called quipu
choices: Knotted cords called quipu
Clay tablets pressed with a stylus
Painted books folded like a screen
Carved stone pillars listing each province
quiz.explain: Quipu held numbers in knotted, coloured cords. Clay tablets belong to Mesopotamia and folded painted books to Mesoamerica, and the Inca left no carved lists of that kind.

quiz.prompt: Two children argue about why so many early cities grew up beside rivers. Ana says the water was needed for crops and for drinking. Ben says rivers made travel and trade easier. Who has the better case?
quiz.answer: Both, because rivers supplied water and also carried boats
choices: Ana, since early people had not yet built boats
Ben, since farmers watered crops from wells instead
Neither, since cities were usually built on hilltops
Both, because rivers supplied water and also carried boats
quiz.explain: Rivers gave early cities drinking water and irrigation and served as roads for boats, so both reasons are real.

quiz.prompt: A city in ancient Mesopotamia kept clay tablets listing sacks of grain paid to the temple. What does that tell us most reliably about the city?
quiz.answer: It kept written records of who owed what
choices: It kept written records of who owed what
Its people could not grow enough food
Everybody in the city could read and write
Its temple was built entirely of mud brick
quiz.explain: The earliest writing we have is mostly accounting. Tablets show record-keeping by officials, not that everyone was literate or that harvests were failing.

quiz.prompt: The Roman Republic began in 509 BC and the western Roman Empire ended in AD 476. How many years is that, remembering that there is no year 0?
quiz.explain: 509 + 476 = 985 years counted, minus one because the calendar jumps from 1 BC straight to AD 1, giving 984.

quiz.prompt: Two students compare the Han empire of China and the Roman empire, which existed at about the same time. Which statement about both is best supported by evidence?
quiz.answer: Both built long road networks and taxed farmers to pay armies
choices: Both built long road networks and taxed farmers to pay armies
Both were ruled by an elected senate throughout their history
Both exchanged regular direct embassies between their two courts
Both collapsed in the same year and to the same invaders
quiz.explain: Roads and land taxes funding standing armies are documented for both. Rome's senate was never elected and Han China had none; what contact they had ran through intermediaries rather than direct embassies; and Han fell in 220 while the western Roman empire lasted to 476.

quiz.prompt: Greek city-states such as Athens and Sparta fought each other often. Explain why historians still treat them as one civilization.
quiz.answer: They shared a language, gods, festivals and a way of writing, and they thought of themselves as Greek against outsiders, so historians group them by what they shared rather than by whether they were at peace.
quiz.explain: A civilization is defined by shared culture, not by political unity. The Greek states shared language, religion and writing while remaining rival governments.

nodes.title: The Middle Ages
nodes.goal: Empires, faiths and daily life across the medieval world.

quiz.prompt: During the European Middle Ages, the Islamic Golden Age was flourishing elsewhere. What were scholars in cities like Baghdad especially known for at that time?
quiz.answer: Advancing mathematics, medicine, and astronomy
quiz.explain: Baghdad's scholars advanced algebra, optics, medicine and astronomy, working largely from Greek rather than Latin sources. Europe's universities and movable type came later, and elsewhere.
choices: Setting up Europe's first universities and cathedral schools
Translating Latin works of the Roman Republic into Arabic
Advancing mathematics, medicine, and astronomy
Printing books with movable metal type in Europe

quiz.prompt: The Byzantine Empire is sometimes called the continuation of one earlier empire in the east. Which empire did it carry on after the western half fell?
quiz.answer: The Roman Empire
quiz.explain: The Byzantines called themselves Romans and carried on the eastern half of the Roman Empire, even though they spoke Greek. Persia was their old rival, and the Ottomans were the empire that eventually replaced them.
choices: The Roman Empire
The Persian Empire
The Ottoman Empire
The Greek city-states

quiz.prompt: In medieval Europe a lord gave land to a knight, and the knight promised to fight for him. What did peasants give in this arrangement, and what did they get back?
quiz.answer: Peasants worked the lord's land and handed over part of their crops or days of labour; in return they got a plot of land to farm and the lord's protection.
quiz.explain: Manorial life was an exchange: peasant labour and produce upward, land to farm and protection downward.

quiz.prompt: A merchant travelling from Cairo to Cordoba around the year 1000 finds scholars in both cities studying the same Greek medical books, written in Arabic. What does this best show?
quiz.answer: Translation and copying spread older learning right across the Islamic world
choices: Cairo and Cordoba were ruled from the same court
Greek doctors had recently conquered North Africa
Printing presses were already common in both cities
Translation and copying spread older learning right across the Islamic world
quiz.explain: Scholars translated Greek works into Arabic and copies travelled along trade and pilgrimage routes, so distant cities shared a library.

quiz.prompt: The Black Death reached Europe in the late 1340s and killed a very large share of the population. Which change did it most directly bring in the years straight afterwards?
quiz.answer: A severe shortage of workers
choices: A severe shortage of workers
A rapid rise in Europe's total population
The end of trade between Italy and Asia
The building of Europe's first universities
quiz.explain: With so many dead, surviving labourers were scarce, and in many places wages rose and lords struggled to hold workers on the land.

quiz.prompt: A Japanese samurai and a European knight both served a lord in return for land or income. A student concludes that Japan must have copied the European system. What is the best response?
quiz.answer: Similar systems can grow up separately in both places
choices: Correct, since Marco Polo carried the idea to Japan
Similar systems can grow up separately in both places
Correct, since both grew out of Roman imperial law
The samurai served no lord, so the comparison fails
quiz.explain: Comparable problems, such as defending land with mounted warriors, produced comparable arrangements in Japan and Europe without borrowing.

quiz.prompt: A monastery around the year 900 holds the only copy of a Roman book in its region, written out by hand. What does this best tell us about books then?
quiz.answer: Copies were rare and slow to make, so few people owned books
choices: Copies were rare and slow to make, so few people owned books
Books were cheap enough that most families owned several of them
Printing presses were already common inside the larger monasteries
Latin books were forbidden outside monasteries
quiz.explain: Before printing, every copy took a scribe months. That scarcity is why monastic libraries mattered so much. The printing press did not reach Europe until the 1400s.

quiz.prompt: Work on a medieval cathedral began in 1163 and the main building was finished in 1345. How many years did that work take?
quiz.explain: 1345 - 1163 = 182 years, longer than most people then lived. Great cathedrals were built by several generations.

quiz.prompt: Timbuktu in Mali grew rich in the 1300s. Which pair of goods crossing the Sahara best explains that wealth?
quiz.answer: Gold going north and salt coming south
choices: Gold going north and salt coming south
Silk going north and tea coming south
Ivory going north and copper coming south
Sugar going north and cotton coming south
quiz.explain: Saharan caravans carried West African gold north and Saharan salt south, each scarce where it was wanted. Ivory and copper moved in the region too, but gold for salt is what made Timbuktu rich.

quiz.prompt: A textbook calls the years 500 to 1500 the 'Dark Ages' because little was written down. A student who has studied Baghdad, Chang'an and Timbuktu objects. What is her strongest objection?
quiz.answer: The label fits part of Europe and ignores flourishing learning elsewhere
choices: The label fits part of Europe and ignores flourishing learning elsewhere
Monasteries in Europe went on copying manuscripts right through
The thousand years from 500 to 1500 were far too varied for one label
The label was coined much later by writers who disliked the period
quiz.explain: All four remarks have something in them, which is why the question asks for her strongest. Only the first uses what she actually studied: Baghdad, Chang'an and Timbuktu were centres of learning during the very centuries the label calls dark, so the label mistakes one region for the world.

nodes.title: Exploration and Trade
nodes.goal: Silk roads, voyages, and the meeting of worlds.

quiz.prompt: The Silk Road was not one single road but a web of trade routes. Besides silk and spices, what else traveled along it that changed the places it touched?
quiz.answer: Ideas, religions, and inventions
quiz.explain: Buddhism, papermaking, printing and new crops all moved along the same routes as the goods. Bullion and cloth travelled too, but the changes that lasted came from what traders carried in their heads.
choices: Ideas, religions, and inventions
Mainly gold coins and silver bullion
Only goods — ideas travelled by sea instead
Finished cloth alone, since raw materials stayed put

quiz.prompt: During the Age of Discovery, European sailors began long ocean voyages. What was a major reason they set out to find new sea routes to Asia?
quiz.answer: To trade directly for spices and silk
quiz.explain: Spices and silk reached Europe through a chain of middlemen, each adding a price. A sea route to Asia cut them out. Farmland, hunger and mapping all came into later voyages, but they are not what launched these ones.
choices: To trade directly for spices and silk
To find new farmland for their growing populations
To escape a spreading famine at home
To map the whole world's coastline for its own sake

quiz.prompt: A merchant buys pepper in India for 10 coins. On the way west it passes through three traders, and each one sells it for double what he paid. How many coins does the buyer in Rome pay?
quiz.explain: Each sale doubles the price: 10 becomes 20, then 40, then 80 coins.

quiz.prompt: A Chinese record of 1433 describes Zheng He's fleet carrying silk and porcelain to ports around the Indian Ocean and returning with spices and giraffes. A student says this proves China was searching for unknown lands. Which reply best fits the evidence?
quiz.answer: The fleet followed sea routes traders already knew
choices: The fleet followed sea routes traders already knew
It shows the fleet was mapping coastlines nobody had visited
It shows China wanted a route around Africa to Europe
It proves the fleet was mainly hunting for new farmland
quiz.explain: The goods and ports named were already part of a busy Indian Ocean trade world, so the voyages displayed and extended known links rather than discovering empty seas.

quiz.prompt: Two accounts of Columbus's landing survive: his own journal, and testimony from Taino people written down later by a Spanish friar. What is the strongest reason a historian would read both?
quiz.answer: Each side noticed different things
choices: The journal is older, so the other account can be ignored
The friar wrote later, so his account must be invented
Both were written in Spanish, so they must agree
Each side noticed different things
quiz.explain: So together they give a fuller picture. Every witness sees from somewhere; reading both an arriving sailor and the people already living there gives a rounder account than either alone.

quiz.prompt: The Columbian Exchange carried plants, animals and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world. Which pairing gets the direction right?
quiz.answer: Maize went east to Europe; horses came west to the Americas
choices: Tomatoes came from Italy to Mexico
Maize went east to Europe; horses came west to the Americas
Potatoes went west to the Americas; maize went west too
Horses were native to the Americas and were shipped to Spain
quiz.explain: Maize, potatoes and tomatoes are American crops that went east, while horses, cattle and smallpox came west with Europeans.

quiz.prompt: A sailing ship covers 90 miles a day. The voyage from Portugal around the Cape of Good Hope measures 6,300 miles. How many days does the voyage take at that speed?
quiz.explain: 6,300 divided by 90 is 70 days at sea, with no port and no fresh food for most of it.

quiz.prompt: Sailors in the 1400s began carrying a magnetic compass and an astrolabe. What did these let them do that hugging the coast had not?
quiz.answer: Judge direction and latitude out of sight of land
choices: Judge direction and latitude out of sight of land
Measure exactly how far east or west they had travelled since leaving port
Predict storms several days in advance from the behaviour of the sea
Sail the same route with a much smaller and cheaper crew
quiz.explain: The compass gives direction and the astrolabe gives latitude from the sun or stars. Longitude, the east-west position, stayed an unsolved problem for centuries more.

quiz.prompt: A European map from 1500 shows the coast of Africa in careful detail and fills the interior with drawings of monsters. What does the map best show about its makers?
quiz.answer: They knew the coasts from sailing and guessed at the inland
choices: They knew the coasts from sailing and guessed at the inland
They had travelled inland and seen those animals
They were copying an older Chinese map exactly
Maps of that period were decorations rather than tools
quiz.explain: A map records what its makers knew and how they got it. Detailed coasts plus imaginary interiors is the fingerprint of knowledge gathered from ships.

quiz.prompt: Pepper cost far more in Europe in 1400 than it did in India. Explain why the price rose so much along the way.
quiz.answer: Each stage of the journey added transport costs, tolls and the profit of the traders who handled it, so the price multiplied as it passed from hand to hand.
quiz.explain: Long routes with many middlemen multiply prices. That gap is exactly what made a direct sea route to Asia worth the risk of finding.

nodes.title: World Geography
nodes.goal: Countries, capitals, rivers and mountains.

quiz.prompt: A capital city is best described as which of the following?
quiz.answer: The city where the government sits
quiz.explain: A capital is the seat of a country's government, which is not always its biggest or oldest city.
choices: The city with the largest population
The city where the government sits
The country's oldest surviving city
The city with the most factories

quiz.prompt: Rivers and mountains often shape where people live and how countries are divided. Which statement best explains why many large cities grew up along rivers?
quiz.answer: Rivers supply water and cheap transport
quiz.explain: Rivers supply drinking water, irrigation, and cheap transport, so cities frequently grew along them.
choices: Rivers keep the local weather mild
Cities near mountains are hard to reach
Rivers cool the land and improve crops
Rivers supply water and cheap transport

quiz.prompt: On a map, 1 cm stands for 50 km. Two cities are 7 cm apart on the map. How many kilometres apart are they on the ground?
quiz.explain: Each centimetre is 50 km, so 7 cm stands for 7 x 50 = 350 km.

quiz.prompt: You are shown two photographs of the same place taken a hundred years apart. The older one shows fields beside a river; the newer one shows streets, bridges and a busy port. Which question would a geographer ask first?
quiz.answer: What made this spot good to build on?
choices: What made this spot good to build on?
How many bricks went into the newest bridge?
Which photograph was taken with a better camera?
Who owned the camera that took the older picture?
quiz.explain: Geography asks why activity clusters where it does; a river crossing with access to the sea explains a port far better than the details of the photographs.

quiz.prompt: A country lies just south of the Sahara with a long Atlantic coastline, and its smaller rivers run dry for part of the year. Which problem are its farmers most likely to face?
quiz.answer: A wet season and a long dry season each year
choices: Frost destroying the crops in midwinter
Ice covering the fields for months on end
A wet season and a long dry season each year
Rivers that flood the coast with seawater daily
quiz.explain: The Sahel has a short rainy season followed by months of drought, so storing water and choosing drought-tolerant crops matters more than frost.

quiz.prompt: Sam says a country's capital is always its biggest city; Mia says a capital is wherever the government meets. Which pair of countries best settles the argument?
quiz.answer: Australia (Canberra, not Sydney) and Turkiye (Ankara, not Istanbul)
choices: France (Paris) and Japan (Tokyo)
Egypt (Cairo) and Russia (Moscow)
Argentina (Buenos Aires) and Peru (Lima)
Australia (Canberra, not Sydney) and Turkiye (Ankara, not Istanbul)
quiz.explain: Cases where the capital is also the largest city fit both claims; only a case like Canberra or Ankara, smaller than Sydney or Istanbul, decides between them.

quiz.prompt: A country covers 300,000 square kilometres, and 24,000 square kilometres of it are forest. What percentage of the country is forest?
quiz.explain: 24,000 divided by 300,000 is 0.08, which is 8 percent.

quiz.prompt: Two towns both lie on the equator. One is hot and wet all year; the other has cool days and frosty nights. What most likely explains the difference?
quiz.answer: The second town lies high in the mountains
choices: The second town lies high in the mountains
The second town sits further from the sun
The second town has a longer winter
The second town lies far inland, away from the sea
quiz.explain: Both towns get the same overhead sun, so the difference is not latitude. Air cools with height, so a town high in the mountains can have frosty nights right on the equator — and on the equator there is no winter to be longer.

quiz.prompt: A river rises in the mountains, crosses three countries and reaches the sea. The country furthest upstream builds a large dam. Which country is likely to complain first, and why?
quiz.answer: The country furthest downstream, which now receives less water
choices: The country furthest downstream, which now receives less water
The country with the dam, because dams cost a great deal to build
The country nearest the mountains, because of melting snow
No country, because the river refills itself from rain each winter
quiz.explain: Rivers ignore borders. Whoever is upstream controls the flow, which is why treaties about shared rivers are so common and so hard to write.

quiz.prompt: Two world maps use different projections, and on one of them Greenland looks as large as Africa. Explain why a flat map cannot get both sizes and shapes right.
quiz.answer: The Earth is a curved globe, so flattening it has to stretch something; a projection that keeps shapes and directions right stretches sizes badly near the poles, which is why Greenland can look as big as Africa when it is fourteen times smaller.
quiz.explain: Every flat map trades one kind of accuracy for another. Knowing which trade a map has made is part of reading it.

nodes.title: Rules and Fairness
nodes.goal: Why groups need rules; rights and responsibilities.

quiz.prompt: A new club decides that everyone must take turns and no one may grab the ball. Why do groups like this make rules?
quiz.answer: So the group is fair and people know what to expect
quiz.explain: Rules do two jobs at once: they keep things fair, and they let everyone predict what will happen next. They are agreements a group makes for itself — not rewards for the best players, and not something a game needs on paper to be real.
choices: So the group is fair and people know what to expect
So the best players get more turns than the others
Because a game only counts as real if its rules are written
So that adults always have a way to stop the game

quiz.prompt: Rights and responsibilities go together. If you have the right to borrow a library book, what responsibility comes with it?
quiz.answer: Returning it on time and undamaged
quiz.explain: The responsibility matches the right: the book is shared, so the next borrower needs it back on time and in one piece. How fast you read it, and whether you finish, are up to you.
choices: Returning it on time and undamaged
Reading it as quickly as you can
Keeping it for as long as you please
Reading every page before you hand it back

quiz.prompt: A class makes a rule that only the fastest runners may use the ball at break. Some children say the rule is unfair. What makes a rule fair?
quiz.answer: A fair rule treats people equally, has a good reason behind it, applies to everyone including the people who made it, and can be changed if it turns out to harm some of the group.
quiz.explain: Fairness is about equal treatment for a good reason, applying to the rule-makers too, with a way to change a rule that turns out badly.

quiz.prompt: A playground has one swing and ten children who all want it. Which rule best balances fairness with actually enjoying the swing?
quiz.answer: Take turns of two minutes each
choices: Take turns of two minutes each
Give the swing to the youngest child
The tallest child decides who may swing
Whoever arrives first keeps it for the whole break
quiz.explain: Timed turns give everyone a share and still let each child enjoy it, which banning the swing or handing control to one child does not.

quiz.prompt: A town votes on where to put a new library: 60 for the park site, 40 for the high street. A councillor says the 40 can now be ignored entirely. Why do democracies usually disagree?
quiz.answer: The majority decides, but the minority keeps its rights and its voice
choices: Because the smaller group actually won the vote
Because a second vote is required by law
Because councils are not allowed to build libraries
The majority decides, but the minority keeps its rights and its voice
quiz.explain: Majority rule settles the decision; it does not cancel the losing side's right to speak, to be protected, and to win a later vote.

quiz.prompt: Rules and laws are not quite the same thing. Which of these is a law rather than a family or club rule?
quiz.answer: Wearing a seatbelt in a car
choices: Wearing a seatbelt in a car
Taking your shoes off indoors at home
Bringing a snack to share at club night
Doing your homework before watching television
quiz.explain: Laws are made by government and enforced by the state on everyone; house and club rules bind only the people in that house or club.

quiz.prompt: A school changes its lunch rule after pupils complain, following a vote of the school council. Which feature of a fair rule-making system does this best show?
quiz.answer: Rules can be changed by the people they affect
choices: Rules can be changed by the people they affect
Rules should stay fixed once they are written down
Teachers alone should propose new rules
A rule counts as fair when most people ignore it
quiz.explain: Fair systems give the governed a way to change the rules. That is the difference between being ruled and taking part.

quiz.prompt: A town rule says bicycles must carry lights after dark. Which reason best explains why this counts as a law rather than a suggestion?
quiz.answer: It protects other people and the police can enforce it
choices: It protects other people and the police can enforce it
An adult wrote it down on paper
Most cyclists already do it anyway
Buying and fitting bicycle lights costs more than many families want to spend
quiz.explain: Laws differ from advice in two ways: they aim at a public harm, and there is a penalty behind them.

quiz.prompt: A council of 25 members needs more than half the votes for a rule to pass. What is the smallest number of votes that will pass it?
quiz.explain: Half of 25 is 12.5, so 13 votes is the smallest whole number that is more than half.

quiz.prompt: Two children both want the last slice of cake. One suggests: 'I cut, you choose.' Why does this settle it fairly?
quiz.answer: The cutter has a reason to make the pieces equal
choices: The cutter has a reason to make the pieces equal
The child who cuts always ends up with the bigger piece
The older of the two children gets to choose first
The slice goes to whichever child asked for it first
quiz.explain: A fair procedure lines up each person's interest with the fair outcome, so nobody has to be trusted to be generous.

nodes.title: Renaissance to Revolution
nodes.goal: Renaissance, Reformation, and the age of revolutions.

quiz.prompt: Enlightenment thinkers argued that governments should rest on reason and the consent of the governed rather than the divine right of kings. Which later event most directly put these ideas into revolutionary action against a monarchy?
quiz.answer: The French Revolution
quiz.explain: The French Revolution of 1789 acted directly on Enlightenment claims about rights and consent. The English Civil War came a century before those writers; the Congress of Vienna set out to restore monarchies rather than overthrow them; and German unification was built around a monarchy, not against one.
choices: The English Civil War of the 1640s
The Congress of Vienna of 1815
The French Revolution
The unification of Germany in 1871

quiz.prompt: The Renaissance and the Reformation were different movements, but the printing press mattered to both. Which best explains how the press amplified the Reformation?
quiz.answer: It spread reform ideas faster than censors could act
quiz.explain: Cheap pamphlets in everyday language outran the machinery of censorship — a text could be reprinted in a dozen towns before the authorities reached the first. The press replaced hand copying rather than making it cheaper, printing in Latin would have narrowed the audience rather than widening it, and identical copies did nothing to stop people disputing what they said.
choices: It let reformers print in Latin, which more readers understood
It spread reform ideas faster than censors could act
It made copying manuscripts by hand cheaper
It made every printed copy identical, so no text could be disputed

quiz.prompt: The Renaissance is often described as a 'rebirth.' What was being reborn in the arts and learning of that period?
quiz.answer: Interest in classical Greek and Roman ideas
quiz.explain: Scholars and artists went deliberately back to classical Greek and Roman texts, forms and proportions. They did not restore Roman political power or the manor system, and their models were classical rather than early Christian.
choices: The Roman Empire's political control over Europe
The feudal manor and its system of farming
The learning of the early Christian church fathers
Interest in classical Greek and Roman ideas

quiz.prompt: Historians disagree about why the Reformation took hold quickly in some German states and hardly at all in others. Name two kinds of evidence you would want in order to weigh a religious explanation against a political one.
quiz.answer: For the religious side: what people actually read and heard - print runs of pamphlets and vernacular Bibles, sermons, literacy rates, records of preaching and popular disputes. For the political side: what rulers gained - princes seizing church lands and monastic wealth, payments owed to Rome, jurisdiction over church courts, and the timing of a territory's conversion relative to its ruler's decision.
quiz.explain: Testing the two explanations means comparing evidence of popular religious demand with evidence of rulers' material and jurisdictional gains, especially their timing.

quiz.prompt: In 1543 Copernicus placed the Sun at the centre of the planetary system. His model still used circles and was not clearly better than Ptolemy's at predicting where planets would appear. Why did some astronomers still prefer it?
quiz.answer: It explained retrograde motion more simply
choices: It explained retrograde motion more simply
It predicted eclipses that Ptolemy's model missed
Church authorities had ordered astronomers to adopt it
It had already been confirmed by telescope observations
quiz.explain: In a Sun-centred system the backward loops of the planets fall out of Earth's own motion, a tidier explanation than Ptolemy's added epicycles - and the telescope was still sixty years away.

quiz.prompt: Two explanations of why revolution broke out in France in 1789: (A) long-running resentment of privilege plus Enlightenment ideas about rights; (B) a bankrupt treasury after costly wars, together with a bad harvest and high bread prices. A historian who accepts both would most likely argue:
quiz.answer: Long-run conditions made a revolt possible while the short-run crisis set its timing
choices: The two accounts are describing different revolutions
Explanation B rules out any role for political ideas
The Revolution had no causes that can now be recovered
Long-run conditions made a revolt possible while the short-run crisis set its timing
quiz.explain: Historians commonly separate underlying conditions, which make an event possible, from triggers, which explain why it happened in that particular year.

quiz.prompt: A pamphlet printed in Wittenberg in 1520 sold thousands of copies within weeks. A student says this proves most Germans agreed with it. What is the weakness in that inference?
quiz.answer: Sales measure reach, not agreement; buyers included opponents and the curious
choices: Sales measure reach, not agreement; buyers included opponents and the curious
Printing figures from that period were invented later
Pamphlets were read aloud to groups, so the number of copies sold overstates the audience
Wittenberg had no press capable of thousands of copies
quiz.explain: Circulation tells you a text was available and discussed. Turning that into a measure of opinion needs separate evidence, such as what readers then did.

quiz.prompt: A printing shop can set and print 1,500 pages a day. A scribe copies 6 pages a day. How many scribes would be needed to match one printing shop?
quiz.explain: 1,500 divided by 6 is 250. That collapse in the cost of a page is why the press reshaped religion, science and politics together.

quiz.prompt: Two explanations of the rapid Spanish conquest of the Aztec empire: (A) superior Spanish weapons and horses; (B) epidemic disease plus alliances with peoples who resented Aztec rule. Which evidence would best decide between them?
quiz.answer: Records of population collapse and of allied contingents in the campaigns
choices: Records of population collapse and of allied contingents in the campaigns
A detailed count of the swords, armour and horses the Spanish brought with them
The date on which Cortes first landed on the coast
A list of Spanish ships lost crossing the Atlantic
quiz.explain: Evidence decides between explanations when it would look different depending on which is right. Casualty and alliance records bear directly on (B); a sword count does not.

quiz.prompt: The Declaration of Independence (1776) and the Declaration of the Rights of Man (1789) both appeal to natural rights, yet both were issued by societies that kept people enslaved or unfree. Explain what a historian can and cannot conclude from that gap.
quiz.answer: A historian can conclude that the principle of universal rights was proclaimed while the practice excluded large groups, and can ask whose exclusion the authors took for granted; it does not follow that the principle was empty, since the excluded soon used the same wording to demand inclusion.
quiz.explain: Reading a document against its context shows both what it stated and what it left out, without collapsing into either celebration or dismissal.

nodes.title: The Industrial Revolution
nodes.goal: How machines remade society.

quiz.prompt: Before the Industrial Revolution most goods were made by hand in homes and small workshops. What was the most important change the steam engine and factories brought to how people worked?
quiz.answer: Work moved from homes into large factories
quiz.explain: Steam-powered machinery concentrated production in factories, greatly increasing output and reshaping labor.
choices: Work moved from homes into large factories
Most people went back to farming the land
People largely stopped working for wages
Craft workshops grew while factories shrank

quiz.prompt: A country in 1800 has plentiful coal, rivers for transport, and a growing supply of workers moving to towns. Based on the causes of the Industrial Revolution, what is the most likely consequence?
quiz.answer: Rapid growth of manufacturing cities
quiz.explain: Coal, transport, and available labor were key ingredients that fueled industrial urban growth.
choices: A permanent fall in urban population
Rapid growth of manufacturing cities
The disappearance of long-distance trade
A return to nomadic herding and hunting

quiz.prompt: The steam engine mattered beyond factories. Which application shows how it transformed transportation?
quiz.answer: Powering railways and ocean steamships
quiz.explain: Steam power drove railways and steamships, dramatically speeding up transport of people and goods.
choices: Flying the first long-distance airplanes
Powering the first electronic computers
Powering railways and ocean steamships
Generating the electricity for smartphones

quiz.prompt: A manufacturing town has 12,000 people in 1801 and 96,000 in 1851. By what factor did its population multiply over those fifty years?
quiz.explain: 96,000 divided by 12,000 is 8, so the town's population multiplied eightfold.

quiz.prompt: A factory inspector wrote in 1842: 'The children begin at six in the morning and are kept at the machines till eight at night, with forty minutes for dinner.' A student uses this to prove that British factories all worked such hours. What is the best criticism?
quiz.answer: One inspector's report describes the mills he visited, not the whole country
choices: Reports by inspectors are not usable as historical evidence
The report is a secondary source written long afterwards
The quotation gives hours, so it tells us nothing useful
One inspector's report describes the mills he visited, not the whole country
quiz.explain: The extract is good evidence for the mills the inspector saw; generalising to a whole industry needs many reports, wage books and hours recorded across regions.

quiz.prompt: Across the first decades of British industrialisation, output per worker rose sharply while real wages rose only slowly. Which claim does that pattern most support?
quiz.answer: Early gains went mostly to profits
choices: Early gains went mostly to profits
Machinery had little effect on how much was produced
Living standards improved quickly for workers everywhere
Output per worker actually fell during this period
quiz.explain: When production per worker climbs much faster than pay, the extra value is going somewhere else - largely to profits and reinvestment - which is why the 'standard of living' debate exists.

quiz.prompt: In 1830 a canal barge moves goods at 3 miles per hour and a railway train at 24 miles per hour. For a journey of 72 miles, how many hours longer does the barge take?
quiz.explain: 72 divided by 3 is 24 hours; 72 divided by 24 is 3 hours. The difference is 21 hours, which is why railways destroyed canal freight within a generation.

quiz.prompt: Wages in a mill town rose 15% between 1840 and 1860 while the price of bread rose 30%. A pamphlet says workers had become better off. Which correction is strongest?
quiz.answer: Real wages fell, because prices rose faster than pay
choices: Real wages fell, because prices rose faster than pay
Workers were better off, since their pay went up in cash
Bread prices affect farmers rather than workers
Wages and prices from that period cannot be compared
quiz.explain: Money wages tell you nothing on their own. What matters is the real wage: what the pay actually buys.

quiz.prompt: A historian argues that the enclosure of common land drove rural families into factory towns. Which finding would most weaken the argument?
quiz.answer: Migration to towns ran highest from counties with little enclosure
choices: Migration to towns ran highest from counties with little enclosure
Enclosure was recorded in acts of parliament, so its dates are known precisely
Factory towns grew during the same decades
Some enclosed villages later became wealthy
quiz.explain: A causal claim is weakened by showing the supposed cause and effect come apart. Growth at the same time is only correlation.

quiz.prompt: Child labour laws passed in Britain while factory output kept rising. Explain why 'the laws cost the economy nothing' does not follow from that fact.
quiz.answer: Output has other causes, such as new machinery and growing markets, so the totals cannot separate the effect of the laws; the honest comparison is counterfactual, asking how output would have moved without them, which the raw series does not show.
quiz.explain: Reading a policy's effect off a total that many things influence is the commonest mistake in economic history.

nodes.title: The Modern World
nodes.goal: World wars, decolonization and the Cold War.

quiz.prompt: The Cold War is called 'cold' because the United States and the Soviet Union avoided direct large-scale war with each other. How did their rivalry mostly play out instead?
quiz.answer: Through proxy wars and a costly arms race
quiz.explain: Neither side fought the other directly, but their money and weapons fought through allies in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan and elsewhere while both built enormous arsenals. Aid and propaganda were real but not the whole of it, and the Security Council was blocked by their own vetoes.
choices: Through economic aid and propaganda alone, with no fighting
Through proxy wars and a costly arms race
Through the United Nations, which settled disputes between them
Through a formal alliance in which they shared power

quiz.prompt: After World War II, decolonization swept across Asia and Africa. Which best describes what decolonization meant for these regions?
quiz.answer: Colonies won independence and became nations
quiz.explain: Decolonization was the process by which colonized territories won independence and formed their own states.
choices: Colonies won independence and became nations
European empires expanded into new territories
The World Wars restarted almost immediately
Colonial borders were redrawn by new treaties

quiz.prompt: Historians often argue that unresolved issues from World War I helped cause World War II. Which factor best supports that argument?
quiz.answer: Harsh peace terms and hardship fed extremism
quiz.explain: Reparations, lost territory and the war-guilt clause gave extremist parties a grievance to campaign on, and the economic collapse after 1929 sharpened it. The League proved unable to enforce its decisions, and Germany rearmed openly from 1935.
choices: Harsh peace terms and hardship fed extremism
World War I's effects had faded well before 1930
The League of Nations settled the disputes the war left
Germany's disarmament removed any means of rearming

quiz.prompt: In 1919 the victorious Allies imposed reparations on Germany. Some historians say this caused the rise of Nazism; others say the Depression that began in 1929 mattered far more. What evidence would help you decide between them?
quiz.answer: Track the Nazi share of the vote and party membership year by year: it stayed small through the mid-1920s recovery and surged after 1930, when unemployment reached millions. Set that against the reparations timetable, which was repeatedly reduced, and read what campaign propaganda and voters actually complained about at each date.
quiz.explain: Comparing the timing of Nazi electoral support with the timing of reparations payments and of mass unemployment is what lets you weigh the two explanations.

quiz.prompt: Two accounts of the Cold War's origins: a traditional one stressing Soviet control of Eastern Europe, and a revisionist one stressing American economic power and the atomic bomb. What is the most defensible position?
quiz.answer: Both sides acted from a mixture of fear and ambition, so each account captures part of it
choices: The traditional account has been proved right by the archives
Neither superpower had much influence in Eastern Europe
The rivalry began with the Berlin Wall in 1961
Both sides acted from a mixture of fear and ambition, so each account captures part of it
quiz.explain: Post-Soviet archives showed real Soviet insecurity and real expansionist aims alongside American economic and nuclear leverage, so most historians now treat the two accounts as partial rather than rival.

quiz.prompt: Between 1947 and 1975 dozens of colonies became independent states, many of them keeping borders that colonial officials had drawn. Which later difficulty does this most help explain?
quiz.answer: Border disputes and divided ethnic groups
choices: Border disputes and divided ethnic groups
The end of rivalry between the superpowers
A worldwide fall in the number of sovereign states
The rapid industrialisation of the new states
quiz.explain: Lines drawn for administrative convenience often cut through peoples or lumped rivals together, leaving new governments with contested frontiers and hard nation-building.

quiz.prompt: The United Nations had 51 member states in 1945 and 144 in 1975. How many states joined over those thirty years?
quiz.explain: 144 - 51 = 93. Most of those new members were former colonies, which is what decolonisation looks like on a membership list.

quiz.prompt: A 1961 Soviet poster calls the Berlin Wall an anti-fascist protective rampart; a 1961 American newsreel calls it a prison wall. A historian wants to use both. What is the best use?
quiz.answer: As evidence of how each side justified itself to its own public
choices: As evidence of how each side justified itself to its own public
As proof that one of the two sides was simply lying
As a reliable count of how many people crossed the border
As neutral descriptions of the wall, once the loaded words are stripped from each
quiz.explain: Propaganda is poor evidence of events and excellent evidence of intentions and audiences. Stripping the loaded language discards exactly what it can tell you.

quiz.prompt: Two explanations for the Soviet collapse in 1991: (A) economic stagnation and the cost of military competition; (B) reforms that let long-suppressed national movements act. Which evidence would best distinguish them?
quiz.answer: The timing of republic-level independence votes set against the growth figures
choices: The timing of republic-level independence votes set against the growth figures
The number of nuclear warheads each side held in 1991 compared with a decade earlier
A detailed biography of the last Soviet leader, written by one of his advisers
The date the Warsaw Pact was founded
quiz.explain: Rival explanations are separated by their different predictions about sequence. If independence movements moved first and growth had already been flat for a decade, timing does the work.

quiz.prompt: Several empires ended between 1914 and 1945 and many new European states appeared. Explain why saying 'the war created nationalism' overstates the case.
quiz.answer: Nationalism existed well before 1914 in the Habsburg, Ottoman and Russian lands; the wars destroyed the empires that had been containing those movements, so the wars are better described as removing an obstacle than as creating the nationalism.
quiz.explain: Distinguishing a trigger from a cause is basic historical craft: the same event can release a pressure it did not build.

nodes.title: Government & Citizenship
nodes.goal: Democracy, constitutions, and how laws are made.

quiz.prompt: In a representative democracy, how do ordinary citizens most directly influence which laws get made?
quiz.answer: By electing representatives who make laws
quiz.explain: In a representative system the main lever is the vote that chooses the lawmakers. Petitions and referendums exist in many countries but are extra channels rather than the ordinary route, and citizens do not draft the statutes.
choices: By signing petitions, which oblige the legislature to act
By approving each new law in a national referendum
By electing representatives who make laws
By writing the text of laws themselves

quiz.prompt: A constitution often limits what a government may do and divides power among branches. Why do many democracies deliberately separate powers among a legislature, executive, and judiciary?
quiz.answer: So each branch can check and limit the others
quiz.explain: The point is mutual restraint: each branch holds powers the others need, so none can act alone for long. Efficiency is not the aim — the design deliberately costs speed — and the branches are meant to be interdependent, not sealed off from one another.
choices: So each branch can check and limit the others
Because each branch specialises, which makes government more efficient
So the judiciary can set policy when the legislature will not
So each branch can act without needing the others' agreement

quiz.prompt: A country's leader wants to jail critics without trial and rule by decree, ignoring the elected legislature and courts. This behavior most directly conflicts with which principle?
quiz.answer: Constitutional limits on government power
quiz.explain: Jailing without trial and ruling by decree attack the limits themselves — the courts and legislature that are supposed to bound what a government may do. Vote shares, question time and election timing are all real features of constitutional systems, but none of them is what this conduct destroys.
choices: The principle that a government must win a majority of the votes cast
The convention that ministers answer questions in the legislature
Constitutional limits on government power
The rule that elections must be held at fixed intervals

quiz.prompt: A government wins an election with 45% of the vote and says it therefore has the right to do whatever it likes for the next five years. Give two constitutional reasons that claim is wrong.
quiz.answer: Winning an election does not suspend the constitution. Courts can strike down acts that break it; protected rights limit what any majority may do to a minority; the government must still pass laws through the legislature and answer to it; and it faces a free press and the next election.
quiz.explain: A mandate is permission to govern within the rules, not above them: courts, entrenched rights, the legislature and the next election all keep constraining the winner.

quiz.prompt: A bill passes the legislature and is signed by the head of state, and the highest court then strikes it down as conflicting with the constitution. Which idea does this sequence illustrate?
quiz.answer: Judicial review
choices: Judicial review
Direct democracy by referendum
Parliamentary sovereignty over courts
The separation of church and state
quiz.explain: Judicial review is the power of courts to test laws against the constitution and refuse to apply those that conflict with it.

quiz.prompt: A country holds elections every four years, but one party controls the courts, the broadcasters and the electoral commission. A visitor calls it a democracy because it holds elections. What is the strongest objection?
quiz.answer: Elections mean little without independent courts, free media and fair rules
choices: Elections matter less than a strong economy
Four-year terms are too short for democracy
A country with a written constitution counts as a democracy
Elections mean little without independent courts, free media and fair rules
quiz.explain: Voting is one part of democracy; without independent referees, real competition and free information, an election can confirm power rather than contest it.

quiz.prompt: A parliament has 400 seats and the country uses strictly proportional representation. A party wins 32% of the vote. How many seats does it receive?
quiz.explain: 32% of 400 is 128. Under a proportional system, vote share and seat share match closely; under first-past-the-post they often do not.

quiz.prompt: A country's constitution can be amended by a simple majority of the legislature on any day it chooses. Which risk does that design most directly create?
quiz.answer: A temporary majority can remove the limits that protect the losers
choices: A temporary majority can remove the limits that protect the losers
The constitution becomes too long and detailed for citizens to read through
Courts will be left with no cases to decide
Elections will have to be held more frequently to keep pace with the changes
quiz.explain: Constitutions bind future majorities. If a bare majority can rewrite them at will, they stop being a constraint and become just another statute.

quiz.prompt: Two proposals to raise turnout: automatic voter registration, or a fine for not voting. A researcher wants to know which works better. Which comparison is most informative?
quiz.answer: Turnout before and after each was introduced, in otherwise similar countries
choices: Turnout before and after each was introduced, in otherwise similar countries
The total number of voters in each country
Polls asking which policy sounds fairer to citizens
The size of the fine measured as a share of average weekly wages in each country
quiz.explain: Policy questions need before-and-after comparisons in comparable settings, not raw totals or opinions about what sounds better.

quiz.prompt: A mayor says that a court blocking her policy proves the courts are undemocratic. Which reply best states the constitutional counter-argument?
quiz.answer: Courts check whether elected power stayed inside the rules voters themselves set
choices: Courts check whether elected power stayed inside the rules voters themselves set
Judges in most countries are themselves elected, so the courts are democratic too
Mayors hold less authority than judges do
Policies that courts strike down tend to have been unpopular with voters in any case
quiz.explain: Judicial review does not oppose democracy so much as enforce the higher-level democratic decision embodied in the constitution.

nodes.title: How Economies Work
nodes.goal: Money, markets, supply and demand.

quiz.prompt: A cold winter destroys much of the world's coffee harvest while demand for coffee stays the same. Using supply and demand, what is the most likely effect on coffee prices?
quiz.answer: Prices rise because supply has fallen
quiz.explain: Less coffee chasing the same demand means buyers bid the price up. The price moves in the market as a whole, not only for the growers who were hit.
choices: Prices rise, but only for the farmers who lost their crop
Prices rise because supply has fallen
Prices stay exactly the same
Prices fall because supply has fallen

quiz.prompt: Money works better than pure barter for trade. Which problem of barter does money most directly solve?
quiz.answer: The need for a 'double coincidence of wants'
quiz.explain: Money removes the need for each trader to want exactly what the other offers, unlike barter.
choices: The desire to save wealth for the distant future
The need for governments to set fair prices
The problem of setting prices in a market
The need for a 'double coincidence of wants'

quiz.prompt: A lemonade stand sells cups for $2 each. At that price it sells 30 cups a day. It raises the price to $3, and sales fall to 20 cups a day. In dollars, how much greater is the daily revenue at the $3 price than at the $2 price?
quiz.explain: Revenue is 3 x 20 = $60 and 2 x 30 = $60, so both prices yield $60 and the difference is $0.

quiz.prompt: A city sets a legal cap on rents well below what landlords currently charge. What side effect does simple supply-and-demand analysis predict?
quiz.answer: Fewer flats offered for rent
choices: Fewer flats offered for rent
Landlords building many more flats
Rents rising quickly across the whole city
A sharp fall in the number of tenants looking
quiz.explain: Below the market price, more tenants want flats than landlords want to supply, so the predicted result is a shortage: queues, waiting lists and units withdrawn.

quiz.prompt: A country prints far more money while the quantity of goods and services it produces stays the same. What is the most likely result?
quiz.answer: Prices rise
choices: Prices fall, as money becomes easier to get
The quantity of goods produced doubles as well
Everyone becomes richer in what their wages can buy
Prices rise
quiz.explain: Because more money is chasing the same quantity of goods. Money is only claims on goods; multiply the claims without multiplying the goods and each unit of money buys less, which is inflation.

quiz.prompt: Two shops sell the same phone. One sits on a busy street with three rivals within sight; the other is the only phone shop in a small town. Where would you expect the higher price?
quiz.answer: The small-town shop, since its buyers have few alternatives
choices: The busy-street shop, since rents there are higher
The small-town shop, because its costs are far higher
Both charge the same, since it is an identical phone
The small-town shop, since its buyers have few alternatives
quiz.explain: Competition, not the product, disciplines price: where a buyer can walk next door, the seller has little room to charge more.

quiz.prompt: A loaf of bread costs $2.00 in 2020, and prices rise 5% in each of the next two years. To the nearest cent, what does the loaf cost in 2022?
quiz.explain: 2.00 x 1.05 = 2.10, then 2.10 x 1.05 = 2.205, which rounds to $2.21. Inflation compounds rather than adding.

quiz.prompt: A government wants fewer smokers and adds a large tax to cigarettes. Demand for cigarettes responds only weakly to price. What is the most likely result?
quiz.answer: Sales fall a little and tax revenue rises a lot
choices: Sales fall a little and tax revenue rises a lot
Sales fall sharply and tax revenue falls with them
Sales hold steady and revenue holds steady too
Sales rise because the product now looks more valuable
quiz.explain: When demand is inelastic, quantity barely moves so the tax mostly raises revenue. That is why such taxes are good at funding things and slower at changing behaviour.

quiz.prompt: Two towns each get a new bus factory. In one, wages rise sharply; in the other they barely move. Which difference between the towns best explains that?
quiz.answer: The second town already had many unemployed workers
choices: The second town already had many unemployed workers
The second town has a larger population overall
The first town has cheaper housing
The second factory builds a different model of bus
quiz.explain: Wages rise when demand for labour meets a tight supply. Where there is slack, the new jobs are filled without bidding pay up.

quiz.prompt: A newspaper reports that average income rose 10% last year and concludes the typical family is better off. Give two reasons that may not follow.
quiz.answer: The average can be pulled up by large gains at the top while the median family sees nothing, so the distribution matters; and if prices rose over the same period, the real purchasing power of that income may be flat or lower.
quiz.explain: Two questions rescue almost any income headline: average or median, and nominal or real.

nodes.title: World Religions
nodes.goal: The major faiths and their histories.

quiz.prompt: Christianity, Islam and Judaism are often placed in one family by historians of religion. Which shared feature is the main reason for that grouping?
quiz.answer: All three trace their story back to Abraham
choices: They use a single shared scripture
All three trace their story back to Abraham
They developed in ancient India and Persia
They began in the same century in the same city
quiz.explain: The three traditions each claim descent from the covenant with Abraham and worship one God, though their scriptures, law and practice differ.

quiz.prompt: Buddhism and Hinduism both arose in South Asia and share some vocabulary, but they differ in key ways. Which idea is central to Buddhism's teaching about ending suffering?
quiz.answer: The Noble Eightfold Path, which ends craving
quiz.explain: Buddhism teaches that following the Noble Eightfold Path helps end the craving that causes suffering.
choices: The belief that suffering comes from fate
Ritual bathing in the river Ganges
Strict caste duties set out in the Vedas
The Noble Eightfold Path, which ends craving

quiz.prompt: A historian notes that a religion spread rapidly along trade routes and adapted to local cultures as it moved. This pattern best explains how which religion reached distant regions like East Asia and Southeast Asia?
quiz.answer: Buddhism, carried along the Silk Road by monks
quiz.explain: Monks travelled with the caravans, monasteries grew up along the routes, and the teaching took Chinese, Tibetan and Japanese forms as it went. Zoroastrianism stayed close to Persia, Shinto did not leave Japan, and Jewish communities spread by trade without a comparable missionary movement into East Asia.
choices: Shinto, which stayed within the Japanese islands
Zoroastrianism, which remained centred on Persia
Buddhism, carried along the Silk Road by monks
Judaism, which spread through scattered trading communities

quiz.prompt: A traveller in 1300 sees the same faith practised with different music, dress and festivals in Morocco, Mali and Java. What does this best show?
quiz.answer: A religion takes on local forms as it spreads without ceasing to be one faith
choices: Only one of the three can be practising the faith correctly
Religious practice changes very little as a faith moves
A religion takes on local forms as it spreads without ceasing to be one faith
The local differences must have appeared long after 1300
quiz.explain: Shared belief and shared obligations held these communities together while music, dress and festivals came from the places they lived in. Assuming a single correct version imports a judgement the evidence does not support, and the local variation was there from early on.

quiz.prompt: Sikhism began in Punjab in the late fifteenth century. Name two of its core teachings.
quiz.answer: Sikhs believe in one God; they teach the equality of all people regardless of caste, birth or gender; they value honest work and remembrance of God; and they practise sharing with others, expressed in the langar, the free kitchen open to anyone.
quiz.explain: Guru Nanak's teaching centres on one God, human equality across caste and gender, honest labour, remembrance and sharing with others.

quiz.prompt: Buddhism nearly disappeared from India while flourishing in Sri Lanka, Tibet and East Asia. Two explanations are offered: (A) it lost the royal patronage that had supported its monasteries; (B) much of its practice was absorbed into Hindu devotion. A historian would most likely say:
quiz.answer: Both processes worked together
choices: Both processes worked together
Royal patronage played no part in either region
Neither factor can be tested against any evidence
Buddhism reached Sri Lanka in the 1800s
quiz.explain: Monastic Buddhism depended heavily on patronage and endowments, and where devotional Hinduism absorbed similar practices the distinct institution had less to sustain it; both strands are usually cited together.

quiz.prompt: A scholar finds the same festival kept with different foods and music in two countries that share a religion. A student concludes one of them must be doing it wrongly. What is the flaw?
quiz.answer: It assumes a single authentic form where local variation is normal
choices: It assumes a single authentic form where local variation is normal
It assumes the two countries lie close together
It confuses a festival with a scripture
It relies on sources that the scholar could read only in translation
quiz.explain: Religions travel by being adapted. Historians of religion treat variation as the expected pattern, not as error to be corrected.

quiz.prompt: An Islamic calendar year runs about 354 days and a solar year about 365 days. Over 33 solar years, how many more Islamic years than solar years pass? Give the whole number.
